lessons.title: The legal system, dissolution & parentage
lessons.fullTitle: Overview of the Legal System; Dissolution & Parentage
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read for 25 minutes, make a terminology sheet for 20 minutes, complete the case-route exercise for 30 minutes, and summarize uncertainties for 15 minutes.

Texas core reading: Texas Family Code §1.003 defines a suit for dissolution as divorce, annulment, or a suit to declare a marriage void. [1] Chapter 6 supplies divorce grounds, annulment grounds, and other dissolution procedures; §6.001 permits divorce on insupportability without regard to fault. [2] Read these sources with TexasLawHelp’s Divorce in Texas overview, then make a case-route map rather than assuming every family dispute starts with divorce.

Texas separation distinction: Texas does not recognize a legal-separation status. Living apart does not itself end the marriage. Depending on the facts, temporary orders, protective orders, a SAPCR, or lawyer-drafted agreements may address particular concerns; they are not interchangeable and do not create a Texas legal-separation decree. [3] Distinguish divorce from annulment and a declaration that a marriage is void under Chapter 6; do not assume annulment is available merely because a marriage was short. [2]

Texas timeline checkpoint: The general divorce filing rule requires either spouse to meet the preceding six-month Texas domicile and 90-day county residence requirements; special rules may apply. The ordinary waiting period runs from filing and is at least 60 days, with statutory family-violence exceptions; it is not a promise that divorce will finish on that date. Divorce residency does not by itself establish jurisdiction to decide interstate child issues. Verify §§6.301–6.303, §6.702, child-jurisdiction rules, service, and local procedures with counsel. [2]

Study vocabulary: Petition = request initiating a case; service = formal notice; response = the responding party’s filing; disclosure = sharing required information; discovery = formal methods of obtaining information; temporary order = an interim court ruling; judgment = the court’s final disposition. Use your court’s definitions, forms, deadlines, and service rules rather than treating this learning glossary as procedural instructions.

Texas practice case • fictional: Morgan and Riley were never married, live in Texas, and have a child. Riley seeks a parenting schedule; Morgan asks whether filing for divorce establishes parentage. Identify whether parentage is already legally established, whether any orders or cases exist, and which parentage/SAPCR route and jurisdiction rules need legal review. TexasLawHelp identifies SAPCRs as a route for custody, visitation, and support issues, including for never-married parents; this does not resolve contested parentage automatically. [3]

Worked Texas response: “We first need to verify legal parentage, existing orders, and the proper court. A divorce is not the starting assumption when the parents were never married. I can organize the parenting questions, but independent counsel should identify the correct filing and any parentage determination.” Research the applicable petition, service, response, disclosure/discovery, temporary orders, mediation, hearing, and final orders. Do not use the divorce waiting period as a universal SAPCR deadline.

points.t: Texas Family Code §1.003: divorce, annulment, or a suit to declare a marriage void. Divorce on insupportability needs no fault (§6.001).
Texas has no legal-separation status. Temporary orders, protective orders, a SAPCR, or lawyer-drafted agreements may address specific concerns.
Filing requires 6 months’ Texas domicile and 90 days in the county. The 60-day waiting period is a minimum, not a finish date.
Petition, service, response, disclosure, discovery, temporary order, judgment. Use your court’s own definitions and rules.

lessons.title: Conservatorship & parenting plans
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the original Module 1 parenting bullet and local court definitions for 25 minutes; separate issues for 20 minutes; draft questions for 30 minutes; review for 15 minutes.

Core distinction: The syllabus separates legal versus physical custody, decision-making authority, rights and duties, visitation/access, and third-party or grandparent rights. Do not assume “joint custody” resolves all of these. Record the local terms for custody or conservatorship and who has authority for school, health care, and other decisions. Third-party rights require separate legal verification.

Texas legal checkpoint: Chapter 153 separates conservatorship, possession, and access. Section 153.002 makes the child’s best interest the court’s primary consideration for these issues, subject to the applicable statutory framework; §153.001(b) prohibits conditioning court-ordered possession or access on payment of child support. [4] For nonparent claims, read In re C.J.C. and the amended §153.002 companion in Texas Case Law before assuming equal legal standing.

Practice case • fictional: Both parents say “We want equal custody.” One works nights; the other proposes sole authority over schooling. List at least four separate issues before discussing schedules.

Worked example: Separate overnight arrangements, transportation, school decisions, and medical decisions. Also ask about holidays, information access, existing orders, and safety. A neutral question is: “When you say equal custody, do you mean time, authority, or both?” A promise that equal time creates equal legal authority is not an acceptable answer.

Deliverable: Make a parenting-issue inventory with columns for issue, each parent’s concern, information needed, and local-law question. Keep preferences distinct from legal entitlements.

points.t: Legal vs. physical custody, decision-making authority, rights and duties, access, and third-party rights are distinct issues.
Chapter 153: the child’s best interest is the court’s primary consideration for conservatorship, possession, and access (§153.002).
Court-ordered possession or access cannot be conditioned on paying child support (§153.001(b)).
Third-party and grandparent claims need separate legal verification. Read In re C.J.C. before assuming equal standing.

lessons.title: Property, support & tax
lessons.fullTitle: Financial & Property Allocation; Support & Tax Implications
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read for 25 minutes; create an inventory for 20 minutes; analyze the example for 30 minutes; record referrals for 15 minutes.

Core approach: Follow the syllabus sequence: identify assets and debts; investigate characterization as separate, marital, or community property; obtain support for valuation; then consider division options under the governing law. Do not treat the name on an account as a complete ownership analysis. Research the applicable equitable-distribution or community-property rules before evaluating proposals.

Texas case reading: Read Eggemeyer for the limit on judicial divestiture of separate realty, Murff for discretionary community-property division, and Milner for ambiguous business-transfer language in a divorce MSA. The briefs in Texas Case Law explain the separate issues and limits; none supplies a guaranteed outcome in a new case. [5, 6, 7]

Support worksheet: Locate the jurisdiction’s official child-support guidelines and calculator. Record income definitions, parenting-time inputs, allowable adjustments, effective date, and any deviation rules. Research spousal maintenance/alimony separately. Practice entering fictional inputs only after finding an official local tool; this workbook does not provide a universal support formula.

Federal tax reference: IRS Topic 452 states that child support is not deductible and is not income to the recipient. Alimony treatment depends on when the governing instrument was executed and on qualifying modifications; payments under post-2018 instruments generally are neither deductible by the payer nor included in the recipient’s income. [8]

Practice case • fictional: A couple has a home, retirement account, inherited funds mixed with joint savings, and credit-card debt. One says, “Just split every balance in half and let whoever pays support claim the child.” Identify missing evidence and referral questions; do not calculate an entitlement.

Worked example: Seek title and loan records, acquisition dates, account statements, inheritance/tracing records, valuation evidence, and retirement-plan information. Flag disputed classification and retirement transfers for counsel; flag filing status, dependent-related benefits, basis, and instrument dates for a tax professional. IRS Publication 504 covers filing status, dependents, alimony, retirement arrangements, and property settlements; read the relevant sections before assuming equal balances have equivalent tax consequences. [9]

Boundary script • illustrative: “I can help organize information and options. I cannot determine your legal entitlement or recommend a tax position. Please obtain independent advice before relying on this proposal.”

points.t: Identify assets and debts → characterize (separate vs. community) → support the valuation → then consider division options.
Eggemeyer: limits on divesting separate realty. Murff: discretionary community division. Milner: ambiguous MSA business-transfer terms.
Use the official Texas guidelines and calculator. Research spousal maintenance separately; there is no universal formula.
IRS Topic 452: child support is not deductible or income. Post-2018 alimony is generally neither deductible nor income.

Do not endorse the trade. Review Lesson 1C.

test.explain: One point per distinct relevant evidence category, such as title/acquisition or classification records; loan/debt statements; reliable valuation information; retirement statements and plan requirements. Two synonyms for the same record category count once. Review Lesson 1C and Worksheet B.

lessons.title: Family systems theory
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read for 25 minutes; map an interaction for 20 minutes; write alternative responses for 30 minutes; reflect for 15 minutes.

Core reading: Bowen family systems theory views the family as an emotional unit with interdependent interactions. Use it as a theoretical lens for observing patterns, not as proof about a particular family or a basis for clinical diagnosis. [10]

Practice case • fictional: Jordan criticizes Casey’s lateness. Casey stops responding. Jordan asks their child to find out Casey’s plans. Write the observable sequence, the impact on the child, and a possible interruption of the pattern. Do not conclude that each person bears equal responsibility, particularly if intimidation is present.

Worked example: “Criticism → withdrawal → child recruited as messenger → more uncertainty.” A proposed interruption is an adult-to-adult scheduling channel, if safe. Describe “missed replies” rather than “uncaring parent.” Children should not carry messages or gather information between households. [11]

Notebook tool: Use five columns: trigger; observable response; next response; affected person; safer alternative. Include extended family, cultural context, finances, and practical constraints without treating them as explanations that excuse harmful behavior.

points.t: Bowen theory sees the family as an emotional unit of interdependent interactions. It is a lens for patterns, not a diagnosis.
Write “missed replies,” not “uncaring parent.” Record what people do, in the order it happens.
Children should not carry messages or gather information between households.
Trigger · observable response · next response · affected person · safer alternative.

lessons.title: Separation, readiness & high conflict
lessons.fullTitle: Psychological Stages of Separation; High-Conflict Personalities
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review the syllabus for 25 minutes; identify emotions and interests for 20 minutes; write and rehearse a script for 30 minutes; critique for 15 minutes.

Learning frame: The syllabus names grief, anger, loss, emotional asymmetry, intense reactivity, blame cycles, and entrenched positions. For this exercise, do not use a fixed stage sequence or label people with a personality disorder. Record what a person says they need and whether they can participate voluntarily, rather than deciding how they “should” feel.

Practice case • fictional: Avery says, “I need this finished today.” Sam says, “I cannot even talk about selling the home.” Write a response that acknowledges both perspectives and offers a manageable next step without demanding settlement.

Worked script: “Avery, certainty matters to you. Sam, this feels overwhelming. We do not have to decide on a sale now. Would identifying the information needed for the next discussion be manageable?” Then ask each person separately whether the proposed pace works. These are illustrative facilitation choices, not a clinical treatment protocol.

Solo rehearsal: Rewrite “You never care about the children” as a specific concern and request. Example: “You want reliable notice of schedule changes so the children know what to expect. What notice would help?” Record yourself delivering a short response; review tone, neutrality, pacing, and whether you preserved the option not to agree.

Safety boundary: Do not treat threats, financial control, or fear as ordinary communication problems. A review of the 2025 Model Standards describes separate confidential screening before consent and continued monitoring for domestic abuse. [12] For workbook purposes, stop joint problem-solving when such concerns appear and route the matter to the safety-screening competencies in Module 4 and an appropriately trained professional. Do not promise that caucusing or virtual participation makes the case safe.

points.t: Grief, anger, loss, and emotional asymmetry: one party is ready to divorce and the other is not.
Don’t force a fixed stage sequence or label a personality disorder. Record stated needs and capacity to participate.
Reframe blame into a specific concern and request. Offer a manageable next step instead of demanding settlement.
Threats, financial control, or fear are not communication problems. Stop joint problem-solving and go to Module 4.

lessons.title: Extended family & broader disputes
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review the four dispute settings for 25 minutes; identify participants and authority for 20 minutes; prepare a meeting agenda for 30 minutes; check limits for 15 minutes.

Four transfer exercises • fictional:

  • Eldercare or aging decisions: Siblings disagree about home care. Ask what the older adult wants, how their participation can be supported, who provides care, and who may make relevant decisions. Do not assume the adult children have authority.

  • Adult guardianship: Relatives disagree about a proposed guardian. Identify existing orders, the person’s preferences, available supports, and legal questions for counsel. Do not independently assess legal capacity.

  • Estate or probate disputes: Beneficiaries disagree about a home. Separate grief and sentimental attachment from title, estate administration, and valuation questions. Refer disputed legal rights to estate counsel.

  • Family business conflicts: Relatives disagree about succession. Separate family relationships, ownership, management roles, financial records, and professional valuation needs.

Worked example: For eldercare, prepare an agenda covering the older adult’s expressed preferences, practical care options, cost information, decision authority, and unresolved specialist questions. Include the older adult meaningfully when appropriate; an agreement among siblings alone is not sufficient evidence of authority.

Deliverable: For each setting, write one stakeholder question, one authority question, one missing fact, and one referral category. Keep mediation distinct from therapy, capacity evaluation, and legal representation.

points.t: Ask what the older adult wants and who may decide. Don’t assume the adult children have authority.
Identify orders, the person’s preferences, and supports. Don’t assess legal capacity yourself.
Separate grief and attachment from title, administration, and valuation. Refer rights to estate counsel.
Separate relationships, ownership, management roles, financial records, and valuation needs.

lessons.title: Extension: blended families & stepfamilies
lessons.html:
45-minute optional guide: Read for 15 minutes; map the households for 10 minutes; complete the practice case for 15 minutes; check legal limits for 5 minutes. This extension sits outside the 44-hour plan.

Core reading: AAP parent guidance treats becoming a stepfamily as a process that takes time and deliberate effort, especially from the parents, and notes that children adjust at different rates. It suggests a stepparent build a relationship with the child gradually and separately from the parent’s own relationship with the child. [13] Privacy and personal space often become important issues when stepsiblings share a home or visit on weekends. [14] Use these points as parent-education references, not rules a mediator imposes.

Why it matters in mediation: A remarriage, a new partner moving in, a new baby, or stepsiblings joining a household often prompts requests to change an existing parenting plan. Typical issues include who attends exchanges, differing house rules and discipline, shared bedrooms and privacy, coordinating several children’s schedules across more than two households, introductions of new partners, and loyalty conflicts in which a child feels that liking a stepparent betrays the other parent.

  • Parties versus participants: In a parenting dispute the parents (or other parties to the case) are the decision-makers. A stepparent or new partner may attend only if both parties agree after separate screening, and the role must be defined in advance, for example limited to transportation logistics.

  • Child focus: Ask about each child’s routines, private space, and one-on-one time with the parent. Do not ask a child to rank the households or to choose between a parent and a stepparent.

  • Communication channel: Keep scheduling and parenting decisions adult-to-adult between the parents unless both agree on another arrangement. A stepparent should not become a messenger by default, just as a child should not.

  • Safety: A new adult in the home can raise safety concerns or allegations. These go to the Module 4 screening and reporting protocols, not to joint bargaining.

Texas legal checkpoint: Texas Family Code §102.003 lists who may file an original suit affecting the parent-child relationship. Some nonparent categories turn on time spent caring for, or living with, the child, and the residence-based category has required, among other things, that the child’s parent, guardian, or managing conservator be deceased. §102.005 separately lists a stepparent among those who may file a suit requesting adoption. These provisions were amended in 2025 and renumbered, so verify the current text with counsel. [15] The workbook point: a stepparent’s day-to-day role does not by itself create possession, access, or decision-making rights. Do not draft terms that assign a stepparent legal authority without legal review.

Practice case • fictional: Dana and Drew divorced three years ago and share Mia, age 10. Drew has married Robin, whose children (ages 12 and 7) stay with Drew and Robin on alternating weekends. Mia now shares a room with Robin’s 12-year-old on those weekends and says Robin enforces rules she has never had. Dana proposes a clause that “Robin shall not discipline Mia” and wants Robin excluded from exchanges. Drew wants Robin to handle Friday pickups because of his work schedule. Identify the parties, each person’s interests, child-focused questions, and the legal questions to refer out.

Worked example: The parties are Dana and Drew. Robin joins only if both agree, with a defined role. Possible interests: Dana wants Mia to be comfortable, to be informed, and not to feel replaced; Drew needs workable logistics and wants his household to integrate; Mia needs privacy and predictable time with her father. Options to explore: Robin as an agreed designated person for Friday pickups with advance notice; the parents discussing discipline expectations directly with each other; regular one-on-one time between Drew and Mia; a private space or storage for Mia on shared weekends; and a review date. Avoid labeling Robin as the problem, asking Mia to choose, or drafting a clause that gives Robin decision-making authority. Refer the designated-person wording to counsel, and suggest a family therapist if adjustment concerns persist.

Deliverable: Draw a household map (members, homes, and weekly schedule), list each person as party, participant, or affected non-participant, and write three neutral questions for the next session.

Extension self-check: Answers are in Answer Sheets & Review under Extension Self-Check Answers.

1. True or false: A stepparent who handles daily care automatically has Texas legal rights to possession of the child.

2. Name two conditions you would confirm before a new partner joins a parenting session.

Build the relationship with the child gradually and separately from the parent’s own relationship with the child.
Parents decide. A new partner attends only if both agree after screening, with a role defined in advance.
A stepparent’s daily role doesn’t create possession or decision rights. Standing rules in Chapter 102 changed in 2025.

modules.intro: Learning outcomes: Gather developmentally relevant information; draft child-centered planning options; identify medical, educational, and long-term support needs; keep children out of adult conflict.

lessons.title: Developmental stages
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the AAP parent reference for 25 minutes; build a child-needs profile for 20 minutes; compare age-based prompts for 30 minutes; review assumptions for 15 minutes.

Core reading: Children’s responses vary with age, development, personality, and family circumstances. Familiar routines, reassurance, and steady relationships can support adjustment; young children may show changes in sleep, eating, toileting, or clinginess. Do not infer a diagnosis from an isolated behavior. [11]

Developmental reference prompts • learning tool, not custody prescriptions:

  • Infants: Ask about feeding, sleep, soothing, familiar caregivers, and medical needs.

  • Toddlers: Ask about transition distress, predictable routines, comfort objects, and caregiving familiarity.

  • School-age children: Ask about school continuity, friendships, activities, transport, homework, and what the child understands about the separation.

  • Adolescents: Ask about school demands, peers, activities, privacy, and appropriate participation in planning without assigning adult responsibility.

These prompts help gather information; they do not specify a universally correct overnight schedule. Keep the child’s individual needs, safety, established relationships, and specialist input central.

Practice case • fictional: A toddler struggles with transitions while a teen wants to keep a weekend activity. Write three questions for each child’s parents. Then identify one assumption you must avoid.

Worked example: For the toddler, ask about routines, transition conditions, and who can provide familiar care. For the teen, ask about the activity schedule, transport, and how preferences can be heard without making the teen choose a parent. Avoid assuming the siblings need identical schedules.

points.t: Ask about feeding, sleep, soothing, familiar caregivers, and medical needs.
Ask about transition distress, predictable routines, comfort objects, and familiar care.
Ask about school continuity, friends, activities, transport, homework, and what the child understands.
Ask about school, peers, activities, privacy, and a voice in planning without adult responsibility.

lessons.title: Parenting plan design
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review Lesson 1B for 25 minutes; list child needs for 20 minutes; draft a sample plan for 30 minutes; test it against practical constraints for 15 minutes.

Planning guide: AAP parent guidance emphasizes routines, direct adult communication, continuity of school and community relationships, and sharing health and school information between households. [11] Translate those principles into explicit options for regular time, holidays, transitions, decision authority, transportation, information exchange, and review. Legal authority and enforceability must still be checked locally.

Practice case • fictional: Lee, age 8, attends school near Parent A, has Tuesday therapy, and spends Saturday mornings at soccer. Both parents live nearby. Assume only for this exercise that screening has found no safety barrier; this does not replace screening in a real case. Draft an option that preserves activities and defines handoffs.

Worked sample • discussion draft, not an approved agreement: During this trial option, Lee stays with Parent A on school nights and Parent B from Friday school pickup to Sunday at 5 p.m. Parent B handles Saturday soccer transport. Parent A handles Tuesday therapy transport. Sunday handoff is at the agreed community-center entrance; the parents notify each other directly of delays. They review the option after four weeks using attendance, activity continuity, transition experience, and each parent’s input. lessons.title: Special needs & co-parenting communication
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the IDEA parent reference for 25 minutes; create a care-handoff sheet for 20 minutes; write a communication protocol for 30 minutes; check gaps for 15 minutes.

Educational reference: Under IDEA, an Individualized Education Program (IEP) is the primary vehicle for providing a free appropriate public education to an eligible child with a disability, based on the child’s individual needs. [19] Family parenting arrangements are not substitutes for school procedures or the child’s IEP.

Learning checklist: Ask about medical and therapy schedules, prescribed care instructions, educational supports, sensory or communication needs, accessibility in both homes, equipment transfers, emergency contacts, and continuity of services. For long-term planning, identify future support and legal-authority questions for appropriate specialists; do not assume a disability creates incapacity or guarantees a particular guardianship outcome.

Practice case • fictional: Quinn uses communication supports, attends therapy, and has an IEP. One parent wants all appointments scheduled on the other parent’s time. Draft neutral questions about service continuity, transport, training needs, records access, and each parent’s availability.

Worked care-handoff sample: “Each household keeps the current provider-approved care instructions and emergency contacts. Adults confirm therapy transport directly and transfer required communication equipment at handoff. They arrange provider or school guidance on any training needs and verify records-access and decision-authority rules.” Do not change medication instructions or interpret clinical recommendations independently.

Sample communication protocol • for a screened, appropriate case: Use the agreed adult channel for factual scheduling messages; keep finances and adult disputes away from the child; specify expected response times by agreement; use an appropriate emergency channel for urgent health matters. Example: “Quinn’s therapy is Thursday at 4 p.m. Can you transport? Please confirm by Wednesday evening.”

Review: Children should not be asked to take sides, carry messages, provide adult emotional support, or hear disputes about money and custody. Support relationships with both parents when safe. [11] If communication itself creates safety concerns, return to Module 4 rather than insisting on direct contact.

Therapy schedules, care instructions, equipment transfers, accessibility in both homes, and emergency contacts.
An agreed adult channel, factual messages, agreed response times, and an emergency channel for urgent health issues.

lessons.title: Screening & intake
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the safety references for 25 minutes; write intake prompts for 20 minutes; analyze the case for 30 minutes; review role limits for 15 minutes.

Core concept: The 2025 standards review describes separate confidential screening before consent and continued monitoring for domestic abuse. Screening is not satisfied by asking both parties together whether they feel safe. [12] Explain confidentiality limits before collecting sensitive information; avoid promising absolute secrecy.

Illustrative intake prompts: First establish whether the conversation and any follow-up contact can occur privately and safely. Ask about fear of disagreeing, threats, control of money or communication, monitoring, stalking, protective orders, child-safety concerns, substance use affecting participation, and requested accessibility supports. These prompts are not a scored or validated instrument. Obtain specialist training and use the program’s reviewed procedures.

Fictional case: Devon says in a separate intake, “My partner checks my messages. I can only talk at work, and I am afraid to refuse the proposed agreement.” Identify concerns and write a safe next-step response. Do not contact the partner about the disclosure.

Worked response: Pause negotiation; clarify safe contact preferences without sending unsafe messages; arrange appropriate specialist assessment and support through reviewed procedures. An illustrative statement is: “You do not have to negotiate now. Before discussing options, we need to consider whether participation and any contact can be safe and voluntary.” Do not store these fictional intake notes in a shared party worksheet.

Output: Worksheet F: concern stated; observable information; safe-contact question; confidentiality limit explained; immediate action; specialist referral; information-sharing permission. Record facts, not diagnoses or conclusions that abuse has been proven.

points.t: Screen each party separately before consent, and keep monitoring. Asking both together “Do you feel safe?” is not screening.
Confirm that the conversation and any follow-up contact can happen privately and safely.
Fear of disagreeing, threats, control of money or messages, monitoring, stalking, protective orders, child safety, substance use.
Explain the limits before collecting sensitive information. Never promise absolute secrecy.

lessons.title: Dynamics of abuse
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read for 25 minutes; compare two cases for 20 minutes; write a risk-response analysis for 30 minutes; self-check for 15 minutes.

Study focus: Explore physical intimidation, economic control, coercive control, stalking, child exposure, child abuse, and substance-related participation concerns. TMTR’s family-violence topic list also includes protective orders, reporting, anger management, safety plans, and violent children. [20] An anger-management referral alone is not this workbook’s response to a coercion concern.

Case comparison • fictional: In Case A, parents argue over late pickup but say they can decline proposals without retaliation. In Case B, one parent threatens to cut off access to money and follows the other after appointments. For each, identify what is known, what requires separate assessment, and why identical process choices may be inappropriate. Do not infer safety from calm behavior or the absence of reported physical injury.

Worked analysis: Case A still needs screening; expressed freedom to disagree is relevant but not conclusive. Case B raises intimidation, economic-control, and stalking concerns; joint bargaining should pause. Do not balance a threat against the other party’s communication style as though they were equivalent behaviors.

Child and substance-use variation: A child witnesses threats; a parent appears unable to understand proposals after substance use; an adolescent threatens a sibling. Identify emergency, reporting, assessment, and participation questions separately. The mediator does not diagnose addiction or evaluate clinical risk alone.

Output: Record concern, affected person, potential impact on voluntary choice, information still needed, and appropriate professional category. No final safety determination may be drawn from these short case briefs.

Also protective orders, reporting, anger management, safety plans, and violent children.

lessons.title: Safety, reporting & referral
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the Texas references for 25 minutes; prepare a decision record for 20 minutes; analyze the scenario for 30 minutes; verify reporting boundaries for 15 minutes.

Texas legal reference: Family Code §153.0071(f) provides a family-violence objection procedure for SAPCR mediation referrals, a hearing condition for referral after objection, and specified safety protections if the case is referred, including separate rooms and no required face-to-face contact. It excludes Chapter 262 suits. Read the full provision and refer legal application to counsel; the mediator does not adjudicate the objection. [18]

Reporting reference: DFPS describes mandatory reporting of suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation and directs emergencies to 911 or local law enforcement. Professionals may not delegate a required report. [21, 22] The Texas Abuse Hotline says urgent concerns require a phone call rather than its online form; do not use an online submission for emergencies. [23] Verify the applicable reporting trigger, timing, and recipient under current law; do not delay a required report while seeking supervisory permission.

Texas reporting updates (2023 and 2025): Under 2025 legislation (SB 571), a “professional” as defined in Texas Family Code §261.101, generally a person licensed or certified by the state or an employee of a facility licensed, certified, or operated by the state, must make a report within 24 hours of first having reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected. The previous deadline was 48 hours, so older guides that cite 48 hours are out of date. The duty still cannot be delegated. [24, 25] Any other person who suspects child abuse or neglect must report immediately. [26] Since September 1, 2023, DFPS cannot accept anonymous reports of child abuse and neglect; reporters give their name and a phone number, and reporters’ names are confidential by law. Anonymous reports can still be made to law enforcement. [21] Ask your course whether you would count as a “professional” under §261.101 when mediating, for example as a mediator who also holds a state license such as a law or counseling license.

Fictional case: An intake disclosure suggests a child faces immediate serious danger. Write the sequence of actions without investigating the allegation yourself or asking the parties to bargain about whether a report should be made.

Worked sequence: Address immediate danger through emergency services; fulfill applicable reporting duties through the proper channel; preserve limited factual documentation securely; pause mediation; arrange appropriately qualified follow-up. The mediator is not the investigator. Do not promise that a private agreement can remove a reporting duty.

Accommodation review: For a case assessed as appropriate by qualified professionals, consider separate sessions, safe arrival/departure, support persons, accessible participation, and online privacy. Each requires an individualized assessment and compliance with orders. Remote sessions may introduce privacy or monitoring concerns. If safety and voluntariness cannot be supported, do not proceed.

Output: A decision record separating emergency action, reporting, court-order review, assessment, process decision, and referral. Retain only necessary information and never disclose a party’s protected location through a shared draft.

points.t: A family-violence objection procedure applies to SAPCR mediation referrals. If referred anyway: separate rooms and no required face-to-face contact.
For immediate danger, call 911 or local police. Don’t use online reporting for emergencies.
A “professional” under §261.101 must report suspected child abuse within 24 hours (formerly 48). The duty can’t be delegated.
Report immediately. Since Sept. 1, 2023, DFPS takes no anonymous reports; reporters’ names are confidential by law.

lessons.title: Stages of the mediation session
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the syllabus and Texas ethics reference for 25 minutes; draft an opening for 20 minutes; map the case for 30 minutes; review for 15 minutes.

Process map: Preparation and screening precede substantive bargaining. The syllabus sequence is opening statements, issue identification, information gathering, option generation, negotiation, and closure. Treat the stages as a teaching structure, not a rigid mandate to continue when safety, understanding, or voluntary choice is absent. Texas ethical guidance places decisions with the parties and discourages coercion. [27]

Illustrative opening: “My role is to help you communicate and explore options, not decide the dispute. We will review participation procedures, confidentiality and its limits, fees, opportunities for advice, and how to pause. An agreement is not required. We will clarify the status of any document before considering signatures.” Ask each party to explain the process in their own words; correct misunderstandings rather than relying solely on assent.

Fictional case: Ren and Alex disagree about holiday transport and uncovered child expenses. Assume qualified screening finds this practice case appropriate. Create an agenda with separate issues and list information needed before discussing options.

Worked agenda: Holiday dates and transport responsibilities; definition and documentation of expenses; existing orders; financial information; communication and review arrangements. Do not decide support entitlement or modify an order through a casual oral statement.

Closure drill: Rehearse three endings: no agreement, partial agreement, and proposed complete agreement. Summarize what is unresolved, distinguish proposals from commitments, specify legal-review needs, and confirm permissible next steps without reporting confidential bargaining to others.

Output: Opening script plus a six-stage agenda with one purpose and one neutral question at each stage.

lessons.title: Extension: styles of mediation
lessons.html:
45-minute optional guide: Read for 15 minutes; compare styles for 10 minutes; write four interventions for 15 minutes; draft a style statement for 5 minutes. This extension sits outside the 44-hour plan.

Core reading: The mediation literature commonly describes four styles, and many mediators combine them as a “toolkit” rather than practicing one style exclusively. [28]

  • Facilitative: The mediator stays neutral and does not offer advice or opinions on the outcome. The mediator asks questions, validates each party’s perspective, and helps the parties generate options. This is the most widely used style and the base for Module 5.

  • Evaluative: The mediator offers views on how a court might view the case and points out strengths and weaknesses in each position. The style grew with court-ordered mediation and is often practiced by mediators with legal or subject-matter expertise.

  • Transformative: Associated with Bush and Folger, this style keeps a facilitative structure but aims at empowerment and mutual recognition, so that changing how the parties relate is a goal in itself, whether or not they settle.

  • Narrative: Drawn from narrative therapy, this style invites each party to tell the story of the conflict, step back from it, and build a new shared story that points toward agreement. It is often described as suited to parties with an ongoing relationship, such as co-parents.

Texas ethical checkpoint: The Texas Ethical Guidelines for Mediators state that a mediator should not render a decision, that the primary responsibility for resolving the dispute rests with the parties, and that a mediator may make suggestions but should not coerce a party. Guideline 11 states that a mediator should not give legal or other professional advice, should encourage parties to seek professional advice in appropriate circumstances, and should explain to self-represented parties that proceeding without independent counsel may carry risks. [27] Evaluative techniques therefore need particular care in family mediation: a predicted court outcome given to an unrepresented parent can function as legal advice and can pressure agreement. The boundary scripts in Lessons 1C and 6B apply whatever style you use.

Family-mediation cautions: No style replaces safety screening; Module 4 governs every case. Transformative and narrative approaches can support co-parents with a long future relationship, but they are not therapy, and emotional work should not delay safety referrals or pressure a reluctant party to keep talking. Tell parties at intake, in plain language, how you work.

Practice case • fictional: In a holiday-schedule dispute about Lee (Lesson 3B), Parent B says: “There’s no way a judge would give Parent A Christmas Eve every year.” Write one response in each of the four styles. Then mark any response that would cross into legal advice for an unrepresented party.

Worked responses • illustrative: Facilitative: “What matters most to you about Christmas Eve? Let’s list what each of you hopes that evening looks like for Lee.” Evaluative, redirected to stay within Texas boundaries: “I can’t predict what a court would do or advise you on that. If the likely court outcome matters to your decision, you may want to ask an attorney before we finalize anything.” Transformative: “It sounds like being part of that evening matters a great deal to both of you. Parent A, what did you hear Parent B say?” Narrative: “Setting aside who is right for a moment, how would each of you describe the holidays you hope Lee remembers ten years from now?” A response such as “A judge would split it, so you should accept alternating years” crosses the line: it predicts the outcome, recommends a choice, and pressures settlement.

Deliverable: Write a three-sentence “how I mediate” statement for an intake letter or agreement to mediate. Describe your primary style in plain language, state that you do not give legal advice, and explain that the parties make all decisions.

Extension self-check: Answers are in Answer Sheets & Review under Extension Self-Check Answers.

2. True or false: Under the Texas Ethical Guidelines, an evaluative mediator may tell an unrepresented parent which settlement option to accept.

lessons.title: Interest-based negotiation & facilitation
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review the syllabus techniques for 25 minutes; make an issue/interest map for 20 minutes; rehearse for 30 minutes; critique for 15 minutes.

Learning distinctions: A position is a demanded outcome; an interest is the concern underlying it. In the practice case, “You must do every pickup” is a position. Reliability, work constraints, cost, or fewer difficult exchanges might be interests; ask rather than assume. Listening checks understanding; reframing converts accusation into an issue; reality testing asks how a proposal would work without predicting a court result.

Worked dialogue • fictional: Party: “Alex never respects my job.” Mediator: “You need a pickup arrangement compatible with your work hours. Have I understood?” Follow with: “What information would let us compare feasible arrangements?” Generate options before evaluating them: school-based exchange where appropriate, agreed adult transport, or different start times. These are discussion options, not safety solutions or legal recommendations.

Reality-testing drill: Ask “Who can carry out this plan?”, “What happens if work hours change?”, and “What advice or information do you need before deciding?” Avoid “The judge will punish you if you refuse.”

Caucus drill: Before moving information from a private meeting, confirm what may be shared and how. Example: “May I share the proposed pickup time, without your explanation about finances?” The Texas ethical guidance calls for confidentiality protection; do not assume a private disclosure is automatically available to the other room. [27]

Output: Worksheet G with statement, verified interest, missing information, possible options, feasibility question, and exact sharing permission. Rehearse active listening and reframing without erasing the speaker’s concern.

lessons.title: Drafting agreements
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the Texas agreement reference for 25 minutes; identify vague terms for 20 minutes; rewrite a fictional discussion note for 30 minutes; review role limits for 15 minutes.

Clarity guide: Record who does what, when, where, how confirmation occurs, exceptions, unresolved issues, and intended document status. A Memorandum of Understanding, discussion draft, and statutory Mediated Settlement Agreement are not interchangeable merely because they record proposals.

Texas reference: For SAPCR cases, §153.0071(d) specifies a prominently displayed nonrevocation statement and required party and attending-attorney signatures; subsection (e) addresses entitlement to judgment, subject to the provisions including (e-1). A qualifying MSA should not be presented as a proposal with an automatic cooling-off period. Read the full statute; this guide is not a legal opinion on enforceability. [18]

Case-law companions: Milner concerns ambiguity and implementation of a divorce MSA; In re Lee concerns judgment on a qualifying SAPCR MSA. Study them separately with the governing statutory provision rather than treating all settlements alike. See Texas Case Law for citations, reading links, and historical/current-law cautions. [7, 17]

Fictional drafting task: Rewrite “We will share holidays fairly and pay extra expenses promptly.” Do not invent support obligations, determine parental authority, or add signature-ready nonrevocation language.

Worked discussion note: “For discussion only: the parents will compare the school holiday calendar and identify start/end times, exchange location, and transport responsibility for each proposed holiday period. Uncovered-expense categories, documents, payment allocation, and timing remain unresolved pending information and legal review.” This accurately identifies gaps instead of converting them into invented commitments.

Review gates: Clarify document status before signatures; verify parties understand the terms; check whether independent legal or financial advice is needed; distinguish partial agreement from omitted issues; review relevant orders and the governing statute. Divorce/property MSAs may require a different statutory analysis from SAPCR MSAs; a Texas lawyer must verify the applicable provision.

Output: A marked discussion draft, unresolved-issues list, and legal-review checklist. No sample here is an approved court form or signature-ready MSA.

lessons.title: Codes of conduct
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read Texas ethical guidance for 25 minutes; compare duties for 20 minutes; analyze dilemmas for 30 minutes; write corrections for 15 minutes.

Source distinction: Texas Supreme Court Ethical Guidelines are general guidance; TMCA has adopted a modified, generally mandatory version for its credentialed mediators. Do not label the two documents identical in all respects or describe a private credential as a state license. [27, 29]

Duty map: Keep decisions voluntary; disclose possible conflicts; represent qualifications accurately; explain fees early; protect confidentiality from initial contact onward; do not use mediation information for personal advantage. Texas ethical guidance also addresses declining or withdrawing when unqualified and objections to conflicts. [27]

Dilemma 1 • fictional: You discover a prior business relationship with one party after the session begins. Write disclosure and process steps rather than deciding that the connection is harmless. Worked response: Disclose promptly, assess ability to remain impartial, and follow applicable rules on objection and withdrawal. Do not ask the other party to suppress the concern to keep the session moving.

Dilemma 2 • fictional: A proposed fee increases if settlement is reached. Worked response: Do not use an outcome-based or contingent mediation fee; the cited Texas guidance rejects that arrangement. [27]

Confidentiality drill: A professional asks for your caucus notes. Do not send them automatically. Identify governing law, orders, consent, privileges/exceptions, and legal-review needs. Distinguish required reporting from a general request for details. Module 4’s reporting lesson applies; absolute secrecy must not be promised.

Output: Worksheet H: facts, applicable ethical source, conflict or boundary, options, reasoned response, consultation needed, and protected information.

points.t: The Texas Supreme Court Ethical Guidelines are general guidance. TMCA’s modified version is generally mandatory for its credentialed mediators.
Voluntary decisions, conflict disclosure, accurate qualifications, early fee explanation, confidentiality from first contact.
A fee that rises if settlement is reached conflicts with the Texas guidance.
Don’t hand over caucus notes automatically, and never promise secrecy that overrides reporting.

lessons.title: Unauthorized practice of law
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review the original syllabus and Texas guidelines for 25 minutes; classify statements for 20 minutes; rewrite scripts for 30 minutes; check for 15 minutes.

Learning rule: Use the syllabus distinction between neutral legal information and personalized legal advice. Explain that a source addresses an issue; do not tell a party what legal right to waive, how a judge will rule, or which legal option they should choose. When unsure about your role, stop and obtain appropriate guidance.

Classification drill • illustrative: “The statute has requirements for an MSA; please review them with your lawyer” is a neutral source/referral statement. “You should sign because you will lose custody in court” predicts an outcome and pressures agreement. “I can be both parties’ lawyer today” misrepresents the mediation role. Revise the latter statements.

Worked boundary script: “I am serving as mediator, not as either party’s legal representative. I can help identify the questions and information needed, but you should obtain independent legal advice about your rights and the consequences of a proposal.”

Pro se variation: If a party has no lawyer, do not become their advocate or assume they understand an irrevocable agreement. Identify access to legal assistance, explain process neutrally, and check understanding without interpreting the best legal choice for them.

Output: Three boundary scripts: request for a court prediction, request for support advice, and request to sign without understanding. Include a noncoercive pause and appropriate referral in each.

points.t: Say that a source addresses an issue. Don’t say which right to waive, how a judge will rule, or which option to choose.
“The statute has requirements for an MSA; please review them with your lawyer.”
“You should sign because you’ll lose custody in court.” “I can be both parties’ lawyer today.”
Don’t become their advocate. Point to legal help and check understanding without steering.

tasks: Write a boundary script for each
Include a noncoercive pause and a referral

moves: State your role and refer the legal question
Offer time to get advice before deciding
Check understanding without interpreting the best legal choice
avoid: Predicting outcomes
Advocating for a self-represented party
answer.script: “I am serving as mediator, not as either party’s legal representative. I can help identify the questions, but you should get independent legal advice about your rights.”

lessons.title: Interdisciplinary collaboration
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Review specialist categories for 25 minutes; map needs for 20 minutes; draft a referral conversation for 30 minutes; evaluate privacy for 15 minutes.

Reference map: The syllabus names consulting/participating attorneys, CPAs, Certified Divorce Financial Analysts, child therapists, and parenting coordinators. TMTR also identifies professional support referrals as a training skill. [20] A referral is not a finding that a party requires treatment or that a specialist may exercise authority without authorization.

Fictional case: A disputed business valuation, tax question, child therapy schedule, and recurring parenting communication problem arise together. Match each issue to a possible professional category and identify consent, authority, cost, and records questions.

Worked map: Counsel for legal rights and agreement review; a suitably qualified valuation/financial professional for financial evidence; a tax professional for tax consequences; the child’s appropriate provider for care logistics within consent rules; a parenting coordinator only where that role and authority are appropriate. Avoid diagnosing either parent or promising a referral solves safety concerns.

Illustrative referral conversation: “This issue needs expertise beyond my role. Would you like to discuss independent professional assistance and what information, if any, you authorize us to share?” Disclose relevant relationships and avoid referral compensation or personal benefit influencing the process.

Privacy drill: Draft a minimal referral request stating the question, not the entire caucus history. Confirm consent and legal authority before sharing protected information.

Output: A referral map and information-sharing checklist, with unresolved authority questions retained for review.

points.t: Attorneys, CPAs, Certified Divorce Financial Analysts, child therapists, and parenting coordinators.
Referring doesn’t mean someone needs treatment, or that a specialist may act without authority.
Send the question, not the caucus history. Confirm consent and authority first.
Disclose relationships. Don’t let compensation or personal benefit steer referrals.

lessons.title: Preparation & role rotation
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Read the brief for 15 minutes; prepare roles for 20 minutes; rehearse an opening/intake boundary for 25 minutes; observe and debrief for 30 minutes. Solo learners write each role’s perspective and critique their own script; supervised groups rotate mediator, party, and observer with a qualified trainer.

Shared fictional brief: Pat and Chris are separating and disagree about a home, retirement savings, and school-holiday arrangements for their ten-year-old child. Legal records and local rules have not yet been verified. Use invented facts only; do not import a real client’s confidential information.

Pat’s role: Wants to retain the home for stability but does not know whether costs are sustainable. Asks for school-night predictability. Do not supply a legal entitlement.

Chris’s role: Wants access to financial records, reliable parenting time, and clarity about debt. Is open to options but does not agree to terms without information.

Mediator’s role: Identify screening and readiness needs; explain role and limits; separate parenting, property, debt, and support issues; ask for information; avoid deciding who is right.

Observer’s role: Record exact neutral questions, understanding checks, missing facts, unsupported advice, and whether voluntary choice was preserved. Observe process rather than rating the parties’ personalities.

Worked preparation: Begin with separate screening, clarify existing orders and needed records, then propose an agenda only if participation is appropriate. Do not start by negotiating a home transfer.

lessons.title: Mock mediation: divorce, property & custody
lessons.fullTitle: Mock Mediations: Divorce, Property Division & Custody
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Prepare for 15 minutes, conduct or script a 45-minute simulation, and debrief for 30 minutes. A trainer may demonstrate a short segment before role rotation; this draft does not certify a trainer or any completed hours.

Three segments: (1) Divorce transition: different readiness and uncertainty about next steps. (2) Property division: home/retirement records absent and ownership contested. (3) Custody/parenting: school, holidays, transport, and decision authority not yet separated. Work through opening, issues, information, options, evaluation, and closure; do not invent governing law.

Facilitation challenge: Pat says, “Give me the house or I will not discuss parenting.” Reframe concerns, separate issues, and preserve voluntary choice without endorsing a trade of rights. Sample response: “Housing stability and parenting arrangements both matter. What information would help us examine each issue without treating one as a threat?”

Safety interruption: Chris privately discloses fear of retaliation. Stop bargaining; do not disclose the concern without appropriate authority or consent; return to qualified safety assessment and applicable reporting/court procedures. Successful rehearsal may end without agreement.

Worked closure: “We have identified unresolved information and assessment needs. No settlement is being recorded as final. The next steps require appropriate professional support and clarification of document status.” Avoid claiming an oral discussion changes an existing order.

Output: A process script, evidence list, permission notes, and closure summary. In supervised practice, retain the trainer’s factual feedback and verified participation record separately from confidential party information.

points.t: Different readiness and uncertainty about next steps.
Home and retirement records missing; ownership contested.
School, holidays, transport, and decision authority not yet separated.

lessons.title: Debrief, feedback & transfer
lessons.html:
90-minute guide: Observe or review a script for 20 minutes; self-score for 20 minutes; revise and repeat a segment for 30 minutes; create a learning plan for 20 minutes.

Draft rubric: Score five dimensions 0–2: role/process explanation; neutral listening and reframing; evidence and issue separation; safety/voluntariness; closure and document-status clarity. Zero = absent or unsafe; one = partial; two = specific and within role limits. A numeric score does not override an unsafe action.

Feedback structure: State the observed words or behavior, the process effect, and one alternative. Example: “You predicted the judge’s decision. That could pressure agreement. Replace it with a question about independent legal advice.” Describe trainable behaviors, not personal worth or clinical labels.

Repeat drill: Rehearse the same difficult moment using the revised neutral question. Compare what changed and whether the speaker’s concern remained accurately represented. In a supervised group, the observer and trainer provide evidence-based feedback after role rotation.

Transfer plan: Identify one skill to practice next, one source to reread, one professional question, and one supervised demonstration needed. Use new fictional facts on retest, not memorized phrases alone.

Output: Worksheet I observation log plus a dated revision plan. Retain actual feedback and participation records where supervised practice occurs; do not fill them in as though a trainer attended solo study.

test.explain: Pause for qualified assessment instead of bargaining or automatic disclosure. Review 7B.

test.explain: One for accurate no-agreement closure, such as “No final agreement was reached; these information questions remain.” One for an unresolved professional question such as classification, applicable authority, or safety assessment. Review 7B.

test.explain: One for each distinct behavior with a check: for example, rehearse a neutral interest question and verify it contains no assumption; rehearse a permission question and confirm exact sharing limits. Generic “be better” statements earn no credit. Review 7C.

library.title: Study plan & schedule
library.html:
Purpose: Build foundational family-law literacy, an understanding of family dynamics, and child-focused planning skills through independent reading, written practice, and self-assessment.

Version 2.1, November 20, 2026. This workbook covers all seven modules as preparation for a certified course. Self-study prepares you for, but does not replace, the course’s live instruction, family-violence training, and supervised practice. All cases, scripts, schedules, and rubrics are fictional and illustrative.

How to Use This Workbook

  1. Read the lesson guide and assigned reference. Record definitions and questions in a study notebook.

  2. Complete the practice task before reading its worked example. Compare your reasoning, not just your wording.

  3. Take the module test closed-book. Type responses in the response sheet or use a separate notebook.

  4. Go to Answer Sheets & Review only after finishing the test. Mark errors and write a corrected explanation.

  5. Revisit the named lesson, then retake missed questions with a new example after at least one day.

Suggested pace: 44 hours across seven weeks: one 6-hour module per week plus the existing 2-hour Modules 1–3 integration exercise. Modules 1–6 each use three 90-minute lessons, a 45-minute test, and 45-minute review. Module 7 uses three 90-minute simulation guides and 90 minutes for its test and review. Solo practice is rehearsal, not verified supervised role-play. These are suggested self-study times. Two optional 45-minute extensions (Lesson 2C: blended families; Lesson 5A: styles of mediation) sit outside the 44-hour plan.

Workbook mastery target: At least 8/10 (80%) on each module test, completion of all practice tasks, and no unresolved safety or professional-boundary errors. Any answer that pressures agreement, diagnoses a party, ignores threats, or makes a child responsible for adult decisions requires correction before progressing.

library.title: Texas case law
library.html:
Research date: November 20, 2026. These six selected Supreme Court of Texas decisions are a study starting point, not an exhaustive digest or a legal opinion. The reporter citations below identify the cases; linked pages reproduce the opinions. Read the full relevant opinion, distinguish majority holdings from separate writings, and have counsel check subsequent treatment, amendments, procedural posture, and the exact proposition/pinpoint page before citing in a filing. No comprehensive citator review has been performed.

Use in the workbook: Read the property cases with Lesson 1C; parenting cases with Lessons 1B and 3B; settlement cases with Lesson 5C. Case law informs issue spotting, not a mediator’s power to decide legal rights or threaten a predicted outcome. All practice examples below are fictional.

Property Classification, Division & Drafting

Eggemeyer v. Eggemeyer, 554 S.W.2d 137 (Tex. 1977)

Context and holding: In a divorce involving a family farm, the trial court transferred the husband’s separate real-property interest to the wife. The Supreme Court affirmed reversal of that divestiture: a divorce court’s just-and-right division power did not authorize transferring title to one spouse’s separate realty to the other. [5]

Mediation lesson: Classify property before comparing division options. Distinguish adjudicated division, ownership evidence, possible reimbursement/support issues, and any independently advised voluntary transfer. This holding is not a conclusion that every negotiated transfer is forbidden or that a mediator can decide disputed characterization.

Fictional prompt: A spouse says, “The court can give me your inherited land because I need housing.” Identify the classification issue, missing gift/inheritance records, and need for legal advice without forecasting the result. Reading: Eggemeyer opinion (accessed November 20, 2026).

Murff v. Murff, 615 S.W.2d 696 (Tex. 1981)

Context and holding: The Supreme Court reinstated the trial court’s community-property division. The opinion permits consideration of marital fault when divorce is granted on fault grounds and disparity in income or earning capacity; fault may, but need not, be considered. [6]

Mediation lesson: Do not teach that community property must invariably be split equally or that proving fault guarantees a specific percentage. Separate the classification question from the discretionary division question and from settlement preferences. Do not adjudicate blame or use this case to pressure agreement.

Fictional prompt: A spouse demands an automatic equal split; the other demands an automatic larger share based on alleged adultery. Identify why neither demand establishes the outcome and what financial evidence and legal advice are needed. Reading: Murff opinion (accessed November 20, 2026).

Milner v. Milner, 361 S.W.3d 615 (Tex. 2012)

Context and holding: A divorce MSA concerned business interests subject to partnership-consent requirements. The Supreme Court agreed that further proceedings were necessary but rejected setting aside the MSA merely because its material transfer language was ambiguous. The ambiguity needed resolution before an agreed judgment could be rendered. [7]

Mediation lesson: Define precisely the interest transferred, liabilities, required third-party consents, and implementation steps. Do not assume a spouse can deliver management or partner status just by transferring economic rights. Nor should a mediator assume power to arbitrate every drafting dispute merely because they conducted mediation; authority must come from an applicable agreement and law.

Fictional prompt: “Transfer my business interest” appears in a draft, but another owner’s consent may be needed. List ownership documents, consent conditions, and distinctions between economic and governance rights that counsel should clarify. Reading: Milner opinion (accessed November 20, 2026).

Parenting, Nonparent Claims & Settlement Finality

Holley v. Adams, 544 S.W.2d 367 (Tex. 1976)

Context and holding: This was a parental-rights termination case, not an ordinary parenting-schedule dispute. The Supreme Court reversed and rendered judgment denying termination. Best interest alone was not sufficient for termination; the required statutory ground and best-interest element were distinct. [16]

Best-interest reference: The nonexclusive Holley considerations include the child’s desires; emotional and physical needs now and in the future; emotional and physical danger now and in the future; parenting abilities; available assistance programs; plans for the child; stability of the proposed home or placement; parental acts or omissions suggesting an improper relationship; and excuses for those acts or omissions. This list is summarized in the linked explanatory reference; consult the opinion itself before quoting or citing the factors. [30]

Mediation lesson and limit: Use needs, safety, stability, and available supports as prompts for gathering information—not a point system for selecting a winning parent. Do not import termination burdens into routine conservatorship cases or infer that the child’s preference alone controls.

Fictional prompt: Parents focus only on equal days. Identify school continuity, care needs, safe transitions, and support resources still missing from the discussion. Reading: Holley opinion and Holley factors explanatory reference (accessed November 20, 2026).

In re C.J.C., 603 S.W.3d 804 (Tex. 2020)

Context and holding: A nonparent sought possession/conservatorship over the objection of a parent already named a managing conservator. The Supreme Court held that the constitutional fit-parent presumption applies in such a modification proceeding and directed the trial court to vacate the challenged temporary orders. The record did not demonstrate that the father was unfit or failed to act in the child’s best interest. [31]

Current statutory companion: Texas Family Code §153.002(b)–(c), amended effective September 1, 2025, expressly addresses parent–nonparent presumptions and requires clear and convincing evidence of significant impairment to overcome the statutory presumption, with specified factual findings in an order granting nonparent relief. Read the current text and obtain advice on applicability and procedure; do not substitute the 2020 opinion for the amended statute. [4]

Mediation lesson and limit: Separate a nonparent’s standing to participate in a suit from their entitlement to relief. Familiar caregiving or a claimed better arrangement does not automatically place a relative or former partner on equal legal footing with a fit parent. Do not independently declare a parent fit or unfit, or promise the result of a grandparent-access claim.

Fictional prompt: A grandparent requests guaranteed weekends over a parent’s objection. Identify existing orders, the legal basis for the claim, standing questions, and the need for independent counsel before bargaining about supposed entitlements. Reading: C.J.C. opinion and current Chapter 153 (accessed November 20, 2026).

In re Lee, 411 S.W.3d 445 (Tex. 2013)

Context and holding: In a parentage-order modification, the trial court declined judgment on a statutorily compliant SAPCR MSA based on a broad best-interest inquiry. The Supreme Court conditionally granted mandamus relief, holding that the trial court could not refuse judgment on that basis. Parts of the lead opinion did not command a majority; do not describe every passage as a majority holding. [17]

Critical limit: Lee is not a rule that every signed document must be enforced regardless of child safety. Read the present §153.0071(d), (e), and (e-1): the court may decline judgment upon the specified findings involving impaired decision-making from family violence, or specified household/unsupervised child access by persons with registration or abuse histories, together with a finding that the agreement is not in the child’s best interest. The statute includes amendments after Lee. [18]

Mediation lesson: Do not promise a broad second chance to reconsider an otherwise qualifying MSA, and do not use finality to bypass safety screening or independent advice. Distinguish consent to participate, signing an MSA, and judicial enforcement.

Fictional prompt: A parent says, “I will sign now; the judge can change it later if it seems unfair.” Write a neutral explanation that document status and statutory consequences must be understood before signing, without deciding enforceability. Reading: Lee opinion and §153.0071 text (accessed November 20, 2026).

Case-Law Self-Check • Optional Additional Study

Before reading the Case-Law Review Answers near the completion review, identify the relevant case and explain the role boundary in each scenario: (1) a court is asked to transfer inherited realty in a contested property division; (2) a party treats either an equal split or a fault-based larger share as automatic; (3) business-transfer terms omit required consent details; (4) a parenting proposal overlooks stability and care needs; (5) a nonparent claims equal entitlement based solely on caregiving; (6) a signer assumes a compliant MSA can always be reopened through a broad best-interest inquiry. These prompts are additional study, not changes to the seven module test scores or proposed training hours.

Assigned Reading Library

References checked November 19, 2026. Read the original source for context; the lesson summaries do not reproduce the full materials. Recheck legal and tax sources for the relevant jurisdiction and tax year before real-world use.

  • All modules: Model Standards for Family and Divorce Mediation (2025 Update). Read the published standards linked there, focusing on informed decision-making, competence, domestic abuse, and the child’s voice. The update addresses these topics along with technology and termination. [32]

  • Module 1A: TexasLawHelp: Divorce in Texas; Alternatives to Legal Separation in Texas; Texas Family Code Chapter 1; and Texas Family Code Chapter 6. Read the relevant sections and verify local procedure. Accessed November 20, 2026.

  • Module 1C: IRS Publication 504 and IRS Topic 452. Read support, dependent-related, retirement, and property sections relevant to the exercise.

  • Module 2A: Bowen Center: Introduction to the Eight Concepts. Summarize the systems lens in your own words.

  • Modules 2B and 3: AAP: Divorce and Separation—How to Help Your Child Adjust. Identify recommendations concerning routines, adult communication, reassurance, and safe relationships.

  • Safety cross-reference: Evolution of Family Mediation: 2025 AFCC/ABA Model Standards. This is secondary commentary; consult the standards and applicable local requirements as well.

  • Module 3C: U.S. Department of Education: IDEA Parents and Families. Read the IEP overview and parent-resource information.

Worksheet A • Local-Law Research Log

Complete before using Module 1 outside a hypothetical exercise. For each row, record the official source, date checked, rule or question, and whether independent legal review is needed. A blank is a learning task, not permission to guess.

Worksheet B • Asset & Debt Inventory

Use fictional records. For each item, record description; claimed ownership; acquisition date/source; value and valuation date; associated debt; supporting records; disputed classification; tax question; and professional-review need. Add separate entries for the home, retirement account, inherited funds, and credit-card debt in Lesson 1C.

Worksheet C • Interaction & Readiness Notes

Record observable trigger; response; subsequent response; affected people; each person’s stated concern; information needed; voluntary next-step options; safety concern requiring separate screening; and referral category. Use the Jordan/Casey and Avery/Sam examples.

Worksheet D • Child-Needs Profile & Parenting Plan Review

Record age/development; routines and caregivers; school and activities; health/therapy; communication/accessibility needs; child preferences gathered appropriately; existing legal authority; practical transport constraints; safety questions; proposed regular time; holidays; handoffs; information-sharing; and review arrangements. Identify specialist questions separately.

Worksheet E • Care Handoff

Record provider-approved instructions; medication/equipment transfer needs; therapy and school contacts; appointment schedule and adult transport responsibilities; emergency contacts; consent/records-access questions; adult communication channel; and confirmation process. Use Quinn’s fictional case; do not invent treatment instructions.

Professional boundaries

Use fictional cases for self-study. Verify local law, protect privacy, and obtain qualified supervision before applying these materials in practice.

Additional Readings • Modules 4–7

References checked November 19, 2026. Use the original sources and confirm current law with your course instructors.

  • Texas Supreme Court Ethical Guidelines for Mediators — Modules 5–6: role, conflicts, qualifications, confidentiality, fees, and process. [27]

  • TMCA Standards of Practice and Code of Ethics — Module 6: compare credential-specific requirements with general guidance. [29]

  • Texas Family Code §153.0071 — Modules 4–5: read the full SAPCR mediation, agreement, and family-violence objection provisions. Check this reproduction against the official current statute before practice. [18]

  • DFPS Report Abuse or Neglect and Reporting Guide — Module 4: responsibilities, reporting channels, the 24-hour rule for professionals (2025), and the end of anonymous DFPS reports (2023). [21, 22]

  • Texas Abuse Hotline — Module 4: urgent versus online reporting instructions. [23]

  • TMTR Family Mediation Training Standards and Training Standards — references for how certified family mediation training is structured in Texas. [20, 33]

Worksheet F • Safety Decision Record

For fictional cases only, complete: concern and exact disclosure; privacy/contact needs; immediate danger; reporting question and channel; relevant order/legal-review question; qualified assessment needed; process decision; safe referral; limited records retained. This is an educational worksheet, not a validated screening or emergency-response instrument.

Worksheet G • Issue, Interest & Permission Map

Complete: issue; stated position; interest verified with speaker; missing information; alternative options; feasibility questions; sharing permission; tentative terms; unresolved issues; intended document status.

Worksheet H • Ethical Decision & Referral Record

Complete: observable facts; ethical source; conflict/competence/confidentiality concern; prohibited response; safer response; consultation/referral; consent and disclosure limits; follow-up. Record one sample for each Module 6 dilemma.

Worksheet I • Simulation Observation Log

Complete: fictional case; role; segment; exact observed statement; process effect; rubric dimension and score; alternative wording; repeat result; next practice need. For actual supervised practice only, separately record trainer, date, verified participation, and feedback; do not invent those records during solo study.

library.title: Integration practice (Modules 1–3)
library.html:
Two-hour exercise • fictional: Taylor and Drew are separating after marriage. They have a home, retirement savings, a disputed credit-card balance, and two children: Robin, age 3, and Jules, age 14. Taylor wants to finish quickly; Drew feels overwhelmed. Robin struggles with handoffs, and Jules wants to continue music rehearsals. Drew says, “I worry that saying no will lead to retaliation.” No governing jurisdiction, legal entitlements, or safety findings are supplied.

Sequence: Spend 15 minutes identifying the safety boundary, 25 minutes mapping legal and financial questions, 20 minutes analyzing readiness, 25 minutes building child-needs profiles, 15 minutes drafting conditional planning questions, and 20 minutes reviewing your work.

  1. Identify why joint bargaining should not proceed without appropriate separate safety assessment. Do not propose a final agreement.

  2. Create a case-route and document checklist. Identify local-law questions without inventing answers.

  3. Write a neutral readiness response that does not pressure either party.

  4. Prepare separate needs profiles for Robin and Jules, including transition routines and rehearsal transport.

  5. Draft questions about parenting options only for later consideration if qualified assessment finds mediation appropriate.

Portfolio rubric: Rate each of five dimensions from 0–2: safety response; legal/financial issue spotting; neutral readiness response; individualized child needs; clarity of conditional next steps. Zero = absent or unsafe; one = partly developed; two = specific, supported, and within role limits. Use the model review at the end; an unresolved safety error overrides the numeric score.

These questions accompany the two optional extensions and are not part of the 10-point module tests.

Lesson 2C Extension • Blended Families

1. False. Standing and rights depend on the Texas Family Code and the facts. Daily care does not by itself create possession or decision-making rights. Review the Texas legal checkpoint in the extension.

2. Any two of: both parties agree after separate screening; the new partner’s role is defined and limited in advance; no safety concern or protective order prevents it; the parties understand that they, not the new partner, make the decisions.

Lesson 5A Extension • Mediation Styles

1. Transformative. It aims at empowerment and recognition, so a changed relationship counts as a success even without settlement.

2. False. The guidelines direct mediators not to give legal or other professional advice, to leave decisions to the parties, and to avoid coercion. Encourage independent advice instead.

library.title: Questions for my certified course
library.html:
Use this list to get the most from the certified course. Write the answers you receive next to each question, and correct this workbook where the course teaches something different.

How Texas family mediation training is structured: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code §154.052 generally requires 40 classroom hours of basic training and, for parent-child appointments, 24 additional hours in family dynamics, child development, and family law, including at least four hours of family-violence dynamics training developed in consultation with a statewide family-violence advocacy organization. [34] TMTR family training has a 30-hour minimum, with minimum allocations for family law (4), family dynamics (3), child development (2), family violence (4), ethics (2), and role-play, demonstration, simulation, and debrief (6). [20] TMTR’s online-delivery guidance calls for live, interactive instruction for the entire course. [33]

Texas Law & Agreements

  • Law updates: Which Texas Family Code changes since 2025 should I know, including the amended standing rules in Chapter 102?

  • Legal topics: How deep should my knowledge be on parentage, property characterization, child support and maintenance calculations, service and discovery deadlines, and interstate jurisdiction?

  • Mediated settlement agreements: What must a SAPCR MSA include under §153.0071, and can I review sample agreements the course considers well drafted?

Family Dynamics & Child Development

  • Reading list: What research and books does the course recommend on family systems, child development, and blended families?

  • Inclusion: How should I account for cultural context and for children or parents with disabilities?

Family Violence & Safety

  • Screening: Which screening tools and intake questions does the course teach, and when does a case not belong in mediation?

  • Reporting: What triggers a mandatory report, how quickly must it be made, and to whom?

  • Related issues: How should I handle protective orders, children’s exposure to violence, substance use, stalking, and safety accommodations such as shuttle or virtual sessions?

Ethics & Practice

  • Boundaries: Which confidentiality exceptions apply in Texas, and how do instructors explain the line between legal information and legal advice, especially with self-represented parties?

  • Mediation style: How much evaluation, if any, do instructors consider appropriate in family cases?

  • Role-play: How is role-play observed and scored? My plan gives role-play 6 of 44 hours (about 14%), while the syllabus cites 20%–30%, so should I add more rehearsal before the course?

After the Course

  • Credentials: What documentation will the course provide, what are the TMCA credential requirements, and what do courts in my county require before appointing a family mediator?
